utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber has been requested not to call the witness just yet because OTP has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Just very briefly, one issue to raise. We see from the list of upcoming witnesses that there's a witness Stevo Plejo, witness number 91, who, it looks like, could be reached next week, and the Defence has listed him as a potential 92 bis witness. However, we've not received, and I don't believe the Trial Chamber has received, a motion to admit his evidence via Rule 92 bis. And I think if the witness is going to be reached next week, that is something that needs to be done immediately, particularly since I think there may be some real questions about whether this witness is an appropriate witness for 92 bis. So it may really be a live issue about whether this witness should testify in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say to that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we assessed the possibility of making this -- these proceeding as efficient as possible and that is how we considered this witness as a 92 bis witness. However, this witness is a prison warden, was a prison warden in the critical time referred to by the indictment. So that many elements actually rule out, that is to say, the basic circumstances about which he's to testify rule out his capacity to be a 92 bis witness. We shall review that possibility during this day and resolve the issue. I wholly subscribe to the opinion of my learned colleague that this is an urgent matter that needs to be dealt with on an urgent basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is an urgent matter, Mr. Milovancevic, and I'm not quite sure what criteria the Defence uses in assigning 92 bis status to witnesses, because just from looking at the position that that witness occupies -- occupied at the critical time, it didn't seem to me like he could be a 92 bis witness. However, having said that, I have seen quite a lot of other witnesses here, and some of them have already testified, who, in my view, would have been appropriately 92 bis witnesses because they're talking about background history and talking about cumulative issues without really touching on the actual conduct of the accused. I'm just saying this by word of encouragement to the Defence to, again, take a critical look at their list of witnesses and their status and try to make sure that those witnesses who are testifying on background information and information that is cumulative are given 92 bis status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is quite clear that we wholly accept this suggestion. What the Defence is guided by in its position is the explicit provision of 92 bis which regulates the possibility of the application of that rule and the explicit allegation in the indictment in which Mr. Martic is charged for the founding and the control and management of the prison in Knin. So the allegations in the indictment actually provide a factual base about which the witness in question is to testify, and that -- if that is an action according to the indictment, then this witness cannot be a 92 bis witness, and everything which is alleged through the thesis of the joint criminal enterprise directly encompasses Mr. Martic as the organizer, principal co-perpetrator, aider and abettor of every, every possible action as the basic protagonist of the joint criminal enterprise. And the Defence has a great difficulty of how to introduce witnesses who speak about these incriminating actions of the accused under Rule 92 bis. But we shall clarify the situation until the end of this day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. I thought we had agreed, yes, this witness it doesn't look like ought to be a 92 bis witness. All I'm saying is, the Defence should make up its mind as early as today sometime whether it is indeed calling him as a 92 bis or not and advise both the Chamber and the Prosecution accordingly. That's the first point. And that any witness who is supposed to testify in terms of 92 bis, that the 92 bis summaries be given and notice be given immediately. Thank you. And I think that is the point that the Prosecution is making. Thank you very much. Does that come to the satisfaction of the Prosecution? Thank you very much. Anything else, Mr. Whiting? Anything from you, Mr. Milovancevic, before we call the witness by way of housekeeping? Thank you. May the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Milovancevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you know, I'm one of the Defence counsel of the accused, Mr. Martic, and we shall now start your examination-in-chief. Before I ask you for your personal particulars, sir, I want to ask you to pause between my questions and your answers. That will enable the interpreters to do their job properly.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is essential that we should not overlap in answering and questioning. Thank you very much. Can you tell us your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: My name is Lazar Macura.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I was born in Kistanje, on the 19th of April, 1949.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are you by nationality and religion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I am a Serb of the Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were born in Kistanje. And where were you educated?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I finished primary school in Kistanje's high school in Knin, and the faculty of philosophy, the English and Italian language stream, in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, can you please wait a little after the question so that the translation is full. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. That is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that you completed the faculty of philosophy in Zadar. When did you graduate?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: On the 14th of February, 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On graduation from the faculty, what job did you do?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: As soon as I graduated, I got employment in Oklaj. This is a place on the other bank of the river Krka. There I worked in an elementary school for half a year. Later I went to do my military service, and after that I found a job in Knin, in the elementary school called Narodni Heroji, national heroes. After half a year, I transferred myself to the high school in Knin and I remained working there until the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Referring to your work in schools, what did you do in schools?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I taught the English language and also Italian as an optional subject. It was not a compulsory subject, but there was a group who were following an Italian language course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you started on graduation from university to work in Oklaj, in the elementary school in Oklaj. Near which larger town is this place, Oklaj?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Oklaj is in the area of Drnis municipality. Drnis is a city, or rather it is a large town, because all places in town -- in Dalmatia are towns. It was in the Drnis -- it is in the Drnis municipality, previously belonging to Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Drnis and Oklaj, to the north of it is on page 30, in quadrant 2E of the atlas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you started working generally in your professional career as a teacher, as a man working in the educational sphere in other words, can you describe for us the situation which existed prior to your getting employed and during your studies; namely, the situation in Zadar, Drnis and Oklaj. Do you have any impressions about that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, I could talk about it for hours on end, but I do not wish to burden Their Honours with all these details. But I do wish to say that I was a student of the senior year of studies in Zadar when a mass movement began in Croatia, the maspok.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Repeatedly we heard this "maspok" referred to during these proceedings. This was a political movement in Croatia at the time. Can you specify the period, please.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: That was in 1970 and 1971, and that was practically a hysteria, because there were a host of magazines and papers writing about how Croatia was endangered within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us briefly what was the objective of that movement, to the best of your information?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The objective of the movement was certainly for Croatia to secede from Yugoslavia as a state, and every possible means was employed for that. For instance, I was with Ivan Grga from Donji Seget as a roommate. We were the best of friends, but all of a sudden he practically started disassociating himself from us, his friends, because he had fallen under the influence of the propaganda which was ruthless. And there were a series of events, there were numerous events, where it was quite clear what the intentions were. The intentions were extremely ruthless, so to speak, and practically a number of attacks were carried out against Serbs in Zadar at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your previous reply, you talked about your roommate from the student's hostel. You said he fell prey to the propaganda which was ruthless. What does that mean, Mr. Macura?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: This was a very synchronized and organised action coming from the high levels of Croatian authorities, that is Savka Dapcevic Kucar, Miko Tripalo and the junior echelons, all the junior people who had publicly declared themselves to be Ustashas. The one who was -- who featured most prominently as such was Ivan Zvonimir Cicak. Ivan Zvonimir Cicak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: This gentleman would come to Knin during the war. I talked to him once for about an hour and I asked him whether he still was an Ustasha. And he told me that he no longer was an Ustasha because he was ashamed of all the people who were Ustashas. He said: "I used to be. I was an Ustasha when others did not dare be Ustashas."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: In talking about him, I have to say that about five or six months ago he was a guest on a programme of Television Belgrade, and among other things he said: "I can help you Serbs because I'm a personal friend of Carla Del Ponte's."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. As you talked about 1971, was this just a political movement in the sense of advocacy of certain political ideas, or were there some public political events?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: In any case, it was organised, so that there was, how shall I call it, a large mixed group, mostly composed of students, who travelled throughout Croatia holding different rallies, giving inflammatory speeches, all with -- along the lines that the Serbs needed to be expelled to the other side of the Drina. And along those lines we have the famous statement by Budak, "You dogs flee across the River Drina."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is this Budak?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Mile Budak was the Minister of Education and Religion in the government of Ante Pavelic, the head of state of Croatia during the independent state of Croatia, during the Second World War. And talking about the River Drina, I have to acquaint Their Honours with the fact that during Franco's regime in Spain, there existed -- there was issued a magazine which was called "Drina," and the Croats never lived on the Drina, in fact. However, this was not just Croatian ambition, an ambition of the Croats, it is an ambition of the Vatican. Here, I have to add that the Croats are also victims of the Vatican, because they became the worst of criminals precisely thanks to following the policy of the Vatican.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I will interrupt you now and ask you this: You mentioned that -- you mentioned this sentence uttered by the Minister of Education and Religion, Mile Budak, in the independent state of Croatia, saying, "You dogs flee across the Drina River." Who were these dogs?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Those dogs, those curs, were Serbs, because during Pavelic's regime, there were inscriptions on trams and other public transportation means prohibiting Jews, Serbs and dogs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you referred to 1971, are you saying that -- you want to say that they were repeating these slogans from 1941 then?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This is a very long -- we're talking about a lengthy process. This is not even only from 1941. I have to say that the Vatican is the key to everything. And, as a witness, I should like to propose for Their Honours to just ask to be shown the secret archives of the Vatican. You will see everything. Everything is written there and you can discontinue all trials then if you see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Such a political situation, that political situation in 1971, was it reflected on the life of the ordinary people, the specific people? Did you have any relevant experiences?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I was a student at the time. I did have some unpleasant moments and some unpleasant experiences which I do not consider to be that important, but I can talk about them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, you are being asked to slow down. You are speaking too fast for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I used to be an interpreter myself, and I apologize to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You should be able to slow down, then. You should know how difficult it is to interpret if people speak fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it's not easy for you, but it's not easy for me, either. I had a fellow student, Mico Pavelic. We socialized. We were friends. There was nothing bad between us then, no bad blood. However, when we played football close to the student's hostel, then groups of Croat students would gather to cheer and to root, and most often they would shout, "Pavelic, what a nice name you have. Long live your name. You may be proud of it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why is that name, "Pavelic," noteworthy?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber is not familiar with it yet, I can say that Ante Pavelic was the founder of the independent state of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. That political situation and that political movement that became known as maspok was ended by an intervention of the state in that same period. I hope I'm not asking a leading question.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I know the situation very well, but I can be very brief in my answer. The Croatian leadership was then replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That will suffice, witness. Thank you. You said that you graduated from the university in 1972 and then found a job in a primary school in Oklaj. What was the atmosphere like in your workplace from the standpoint of interethnic relations? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Oklaj is a majority Croat place, where Serbs are in a minority. When I got a job there, there was a trial going on against the manager of an enterprise, Davor Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Because he was one of those on trial as being involved in the mass movement, the maspok, along with one of the math teachers, Pasko Kulusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did these trials end?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They were sentenced to imprisonment, I don't know for how long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they removed from their jobs?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They lost their jobs at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your relations with these people when you were working together? How would you describe them, in one sentence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They did not display any hostility towards me, because, after all, they were on trial at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you do your military service?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: October 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you finish your military service, and were you given a rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I completed the school for reserve officers in Bilice, infantry stream, and became a reserve sergeant, later captain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You got this rank in which army?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the official name of that army?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in 1990, you were a reserve officer of the Yugoslav People's Army, holding what rank?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After serving in the army, you said you found a job in Knin; first of all, in a primary school for six months, and later in the Brotherhood and Unity High School in Knin as an English teacher. So you continued to work in this sphere of education.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes. I continued even during the war. But during the war I was appointed director of the Serbian Radio Knin, so for a while I did that job. And after the war I returned to my original profession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mobilised during the war?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: No. I was deputy president -- vice president of the Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said: "During the war I was vice president of Knin municipality." When you say "during the war," which period do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: After the elections in 1990, those were the first democratic elections on the territory of Croatia, because elections were not carried out in the whole of Yugoslavia, just in republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when did this period last?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: You mean the war in Croatia? Until Operation Storm, until the 4th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to your teaching job at school, were you involved in any other activity related to your training?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I'm a literary translator, and I have been one for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You read philosophy at university. You became a teacher of English and French.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: English and Italian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, English and Italian. You are a translator. Can you tell us: How come you became politically involved, and even vice president of the Knin municipality? At least that's the way I understand it. You became politically active.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I did not do it out of choice but because it was my misfortune to be forced to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of misfortune led you to be politically involved?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: That was the year when the Croatian Democratic Union won in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatian Democratic Union, sorry, not university. Okay.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president of the HDZ was Dr. Franjo Tudjman. He had long been known as a Croat nationalist of the worst kind. And at the time of the regime of Josip Broz Tito, he spent some time in prison, a notorious prison in Lepoglava. And he never made any bones about his wish to continue what Ante Pavelic had started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say he made no bones about it? Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: From all his public appearances, the statements he gave to the press, radio, television, I had occasion to see and hear him many times. And one of his statements, which is the best confirmation of what I just said, is this: "Croatia," meaning Pavelic's Croatia, "was not a mere quisling creation, but the expression of historic aspirations of the Croat people."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, why do you believe that this sentence uttered by Mr. Tudjman is so impressive as an indication that Tudjman intended to continue what Pavelic had started? Should I ask the question, rather, what Pavelic did?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, as for Pavelic, I believe that he had created the most monstrous state in the history of mankind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: As for the crimes that Ustashas committed against Serbs, they horrified even their protectors and sponsors, the German Nazis. While that state was neither independent or a state, nor was it Croatia. It did not even have any economic programme of any kind. The only programme of Ante Pavelic and his state was that there should remain living in Croatia only the pure Aryan race.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The pure Aryan race being who?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Catholic Croats. No one else would have the right to live in that state. And here, Pavelic leans on Ante Starcevic. Ante Starcevic was a Croat politician from the latter half of the 19th century who founded the Croatian Party of Rights. And his programme boiled down to just one sentence; namely, the solution to the Serb issue in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was that one sentence?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: "One-third of the Serbs should be killed, one-third expelled, and one-third converted to Catholicism."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Ante Pavelic implement this programme?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Such a programme was implemented in the most horrific and brutal way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that even the German allies of Croatia were horrified. Can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: There are many of them, but I remember some in particular. I personally translated a book by Dr. Marco Aurelio Rivelli. He has a doctorate in political science, and he wrote, among other books, one called "The Archbishop of Genocide." "The Archbishop of Genocide," that was a reference to the archbishop of Zagreb, a ranking representative of the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll deal with it a bit later. Just tell me one thing. The author of this book that you mentioned, Marco Aurelio Rivelli, what is he by nationality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Italian by nationality, and of Catholic faith. He lives in Bergamo, Italy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the fact that you translated his book make it possible for you to gain some insights and information?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: That book is very well researched. It deals only with facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said a bit earlier that Tudjman intended to continue the work of Pavelic back in the independent state of Croatia. You stated an opinion about the independent state of Croatia. Now, why do you think that it was Tudjman's intention to continue that work?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, he had to because he was financed and dependent on the Croatian diaspora and the Ustasha movement abroad. The main centre was in Munich after the Second World War. And while I'm speaking of Munich, I must say that it was there that the Papal representative there was Eugenio Pacelli, who later became Pope Pius the 12th, and that was Hitler's Pope. Eugenio Pacelli's was Hitler's right arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us at what time Archbishop Stepinac was an arch bishop?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I think in 1937.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Until the end of the war. Later he was tried and imprisoned. But let me tell you one thing about the trial of Stepinac. Tito offered him a way out. Tito asked him to leave the country and, in exchange, he would be released from prison. However, the Vatican did not allow it. The Pope in Rome did not allow it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Because the one who blessed Ustasha crimes during the war needed to be turned into a martyr.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to this martyr later, in the 1990s? I mean Archbishop Stepinac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely why Marco Aurelio Rivelli wrote this book, because this latest Pope, John Paul II, Pope Voytilla, came to Marija Bistrica to canonise Stepinac. And that is one step towards turning somebody into a saint.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Marija Bistrica?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: It is 20 kilometres from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened later?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: He was turned into a saint, and the Pope made a speech later about crimes that must not be repeated, without ever mentioning the crimes committed and blessed by Stepinac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was out of misfortune that you became politically active, and you described your own vision of the policies of Mr. Tudjman. What was it that was happening in everyday life that was the first thing that moved you to become politically active?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Before the war began, Tudjman established his own army, the so-called Home Guard Corps, the ZNG, "Zengas," they called them. You will allow, ladies and gentlemen, that in every country that is deemed to be armed insurgency of the worst kind, because the only regular armed force at the time was the Yugoslav People's Army. And we watched on television that lineup on the stadium in Kranjceviceva Street in Zagreb, and we followed it all. Croats did not hide themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. You said we watched on television the lineup in Kranjceviceva Street in Zagreb. What kind of lineup?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I don't know the date. It was 1990. But I remember the whole incident, the event. The stadium was chosen so that a larger crowd could gather there. It was not the organisation of a secret army. On the contrary, it was very public and meant to produce an effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not answer. Who was lined up there? What kind of a parade was it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: It was a parade of the Croatian army, the army that had to complete what the Croatian army in the Second World War did not do. In practical terms, it means that they were to finish what the Ustashas did not manage to finish in the four years of slaughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, in 1990 and 1991, who was the prime minister of the Yugoslav government?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: It was Ante Markovic. And, in general, when we speak about the war in Yugoslavia, one has to bear in mind that even in the military leadership the Croats, in fact, played the main role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Ante Markovic, the prime minister, what is his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: He was a Croat, and he established some kind of a Yugoslav party. But he did not attend any rallies in Croatia. He only organised such rallies in Bosnia and in the rest of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the foreign minister at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I can't recall who the foreign minister was, but I know who was the chief of the air force. It was Antun Tus. He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name Budimir Loncar ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Budimir Loncar was the foreign minister of Yugoslavia for a long time. He was originally from Ugljan. It's an island in the Adriatic, just opposite Zadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That would be sufficient. Was Mr. Mesic, the current president of the Republic of Croatia, was he holding any office in Yugoslavia at that time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: At the insistence of the HDZ, Stipe Mesic replaced Stipe Suvar in the collective Presidency of Yugoslavia, because Stipe Suvar was the Croatian representative on the Presidency. But because Stipe Suvar was not a member of the HDZ, he could no longer remain in that body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stipe Mesic, as the Croatian representative in the SFRY Presidency, did he hold any function there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, he himself said that his main task was to break Yugoslavia down, and he was the president of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And I have to say one other thing regarding President Mesic. Stipe Mesic married a Serb, and his wife and her sister are the survivors of the Jastrebarsko camp, which was the camp that the Ustashas set up for children. So it is quite incredible. This is something that you would find incredible even if you read about it in books. Life sometimes surpasses even the most surreal elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Macura. You said that Stipe Mesic's wife, as a child, is a survivor of the children's camp in Jastrebarsko. What kind of a camp was it, and who set it up?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, the camp was established by Pavelic's government. It was a dictatorship. There were no elections held. It was a dictatorship, pure and simple. There were 22 camps, temporary and permanent. Jasinovac, for instance, was a system of death camps, a whole complex of death camps. And based on what Andrija Artukovic said, Andrija Artukovic, who was the interior minister in Pavelic's cabinet --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we are talking about the independent state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes. The independent state of Croatia that was patronised by the Nazis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please, Mr. Milovancevic. The camp which Mesic's wife and sister survived, the concentration camp for children, was it also a death camp? Or was it a different type of camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a death camp, like all the other camps. The only thing is that the official Croatian version was that these were labour camps. And the United Nations delegation toured those camps and then they dressed up those small children in nice clothes, taught them some songs, and they presented this false front. But Coradozoli [phoen], an Italian reporter who was with the delegation, noticed some other things in the camp but the officials did not notice any of it. So even the United Nations did not consider Jasinovac as a death camp for a long time, but now there is a five-member commission of the United Nations charged with Jasinovac, and Dr. Rivelli, in fact, is one of the members of that commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, just one moment, without taking away your train, whilst I am at it: You, Mr. Witness, had mentioned before that the Croats wanted to create an Aryan race that would exclude Serbs. Are not Serbs and Croats descendents of Aryans, of the same racial source, genetically, biologically? And if the answer is "no," is there a physical difference in looking at the two in the component? Is one obviously different looking from the next, racially?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not subscribe to the Aryan theory, but this is not my theory, this is something that Pavelic, in fact, took over from Hitler. But let me just give you an example from Split as an illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No. I really want you to answer what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to tell you that a large portion of Croats, in fact, are descendents of Serbs. This is a long process that went on from the distant past. And I can tell you that, for instance, in the Zadar area, before Maria Theresa ascended to the thrown in Vienna, there were 19 Orthodox parishes, 19 Orthodox parish churches in that area, and then she ordered a mass unification. And I will tell you what this term means: "Conversion to the Uniate church." The adherents of the Orthodox religion are allowed to worship as they want, to celebrate their patron saints, and the only condition was that they had to recognise the Pope in Rome. This is why I say that everything actually stems from Rome. And in effect, in its essence, we are talking about one and the same people. And my brother is married to a Croat woman, but he himself had been expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that your answer is that racially it's virtually indistinguishable. One is not more Aryan than the next. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the children's camp in Jastrebarsko. They were pioneer camps, scout camps? What kind of a camp was this?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: As far as Jastrebarsko is concerned, I think it was a much milder regime in that camp than in the other camps, but there were camps for all categories of the population - the elderly, women and children. Then you had camps for women and children. Stara Gradiska was this type of camp, for instance, Stara Gradiska where about 75.000 women and children were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just wanted to get a brief answer from you. Could we call this a concentration camp, or not?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: At any rate, this was a concentration camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I tried to get you to answer my question. You said that you joined politics because of some misfortune and you linked this with the appearance of Mr. Tudjman. How did this manifest itself in the public life?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: As soon as he came into power in Zagreb, Tudjman demanded that all the employees in all the enterprises sign -- I don't exactly know the text of this declaration, but to sign a declaration expressing their support to the Croatian leadership. In other words, you could not even be a mechanic unless you gave your political support to Franjo Tudjman. That is why there followed a mass firing of Serbs in Zagreb. There were some Serbs that signed this declaration and continued to work, but most Serbs thought that it had absolutely nothing to do with their jobs. And I have friends who are in litigation with the Croatian state, have been in litigation with them for years. For instance Glisa Kolundzic, who returned - now he lives in Kakan, near Biograd, and he still -- this lawsuit is still going on, although he filed suit against the Croatian state on three counts: expulsion, the burning of his house in Zadar, and the loss of his job. It's been 17 years now and he still -- he still hasn't received the judgment. And you have thousands of such ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 11 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how did you become politically active in 1990, in what way? And why? Why you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party was established. It was registered just as any other political party in Croatia. Dr. Jovan Raskovic was the president of the party. We saw this party as a shield protecting the Serb people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, shield against whom? Why?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, Tudjman announced that Serbs would have their status revoked, the status of the constituent people, and Saiks [phoen] did the same. He, in fact, was a jurist. And the status of the constituent people is something that Serbs won with their lives, so this was not something that was gifted to them. And the fact that Serbs were now declared to be a national minority meant that they lost some collective rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologize for interrupting you, but you said that you lost some collective rights when you were declared a national minority. What would be the most important collective right? What was of particular importance for you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, when we joined Yugoslavia after the First World War, the Croats, Serbs and Slovenes from the area of the former Austro-Hungarian empire, they jointly decided to enter Yugoslavia. This was particularly beneficial for the Croats because they, who had been on the losing side, now joined the winning side. And they have the Serb people to thank for that, because they suffered the most casualties in the First World War. Then we come to the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just a moment. Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic. Isn't this taking a little too much time? This is background, as the witness is not a historian, nor a lawyer. He is here to give testimony on issues relevant to the indictment, and to my feeling, you are wasting time and you have a budgeted time limit. Maybe you could focus better. I hate to correct you, but it is really sound advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, once the Defence is satisfied that our learned colleagues from the Prosecution know what the constituent people is, we will no longer be dealing with this topic. And once we are satisfied that they know the provisions in the Yugoslav and the Croatian constitutions of 1990 on Serbs as a constituent people, we will no longer have need to discuss this topic. These are some elementary things, but in the indictment and through the evidence of Prosecution witnesses, they were presented in a totally different light. This witness is a direct participant in the events. He is one of the officials, high-ranking officials, a close associate of Mr. Martic and Mr. Raskovic. He is one of the key people in the SDS, and I believe that it is relevant for him to tell us what were the motives that led to the establishment of this party. Was it, as the Prosecutor alleges, the persecution of all non-Serb population, the worst kinds of atrocities, or something else? That is why this witness is talking about this, and this is why I'm asking him why the events in 1990 rang an alarm bell for the Serbs in Croatia. I'm trying to get an answer to this question. And this is --. But thank you very much for your warning about the time. We will deal with this in one sentence or two sentences. Our witness is an educated person and he should be able to deal with this in three sentences. We are now in the Second World War, so if you will allow me, I would like to pursue this topic some more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I didn't interrupt you earlier, but now I have the feeling, and still have that, as you're saying, the witness can give testimony on the actual facts on the actual time of the indictment period. Please focus on that. And, okay, I'm sure, of course, the witness is an educated person. There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about the reasons why Serbs had the status of a constituent people. You did not explain why -- how they earned this status in the Second World War, because you were interrupted there. But why was it a problem for you, this announcement that they would be thrown out of the constitution? If you can just give us a very brief answer.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I will be very brief. In the Second World War, Serbs had two anti-fascist movements: the partisan movement and the Chetnik movement. Now, this is the tragedy of the Serb people: That they actually fought each other. But let me now tell you what Croats did. Croats were either in the Home Guard or in the Ustashas. Very few Croats were in the partisan movement. Let me give you an example by way of illustration. I spoke with Professor Ilija Stojanovic. He's a member of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. He is originally from Otoca, in Lika. Lika is in Croatia. Because he was a member of the 6th Lika Division, a division which has several thousand people, fighters, I asked him, "How many Croats were in the 6th Lika Division?" And he said, "I know the exact figure. Not a problem. 27 Exactly. 27."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 6th Lika Division, it was active in what time period?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: It was the famous division that defended Tito in Drvar in the Second World War. When the Germans mounted an airborne attack on Drvar, they defended Tito there. Songs were sung about them. But just let me tell you: You have several thousand fighters; only 27 of them were Croats. An important thing has to be noted here: Tudjman was one of the people who was in charge of transferring Home Guard members and the Ustashas to the partisan movement as the war drew to its end. And that's how they joined the winning side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, is this not a convenient time for you to take a break, at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was precisely what I wanted to say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned. We will come back at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Macura, when the first multiparty elections were held in Croatia? I don't mean the exact date.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: That was April and May, 1990. I believe the second round was on the 6th of May, and that's when they ended, on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serbian Democratic Party participate in those elections?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The SDS did participate at those elections and it won a majority in the area of Knin, in particular in the first round, so that it was all solved in the first round. And some parts of the Serbian territories in Croatia mostly supported Racan's party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us recall who actually won these first multiparty elections. What party had the majority in the Croatian parliament?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: In the Croatian parliament, the Croatian Democratic Union won with Dr. Franjo Tudjman at its helm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about when the constitutional amendments were proposed to be tabled in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They immediately announced the constitutional changes, but I believe that it was in December that the Assembly promulgated annual constitution, 1990 namely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say they immediately announced it. When and how?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, throughout their campaign they kept referring to the fact that Croatia was only the state of the -- a state of the Croatian people, and then different gatherings were held. And I remember, for instance, Fra Brother Duka, when he talked in the Lisinski hall in Zagreb, when he said triumphantly, "Above the Croatian parliament is only God." And that was a clear message to all others who were not members of the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say the HDZ announced constitutional amendments immediately after their victory. What was the substance of those changes?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, as Tudjman says, it was the historical aspiration of the Croatian people to get its own pure state, pure Croatian state, and to solve the Serbian question in Croatia. In 1996, Tudjman, when the war was finished - so in 1996, in May - Tudjman stated this: "The Serbian question in Croatia has been finally solved. There never must be over 3 per cent of them." And if one takes into consideration the fact that there had been over -- or approximately 20 per cent of Serbs in Croatia, it is quite clear, then, what kind of a message that was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, can you tell us: Why were Serbs in Croatia against a change of their constitutional status? Why was it -- was this question of being a constituent nation that important, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: From 1630 to 1881, we had the Valahorem Statuta [phoen], the Statuta Valahorem, which was actually the Serbian constitution within the Austro-Hungarian empire. And we counted, we thought, as we had been living there for over a thousand years. And that was, both ethnically and historically, our land. We considered ourselves a people on that land with merits for Croatia. And, as we had obtained the status of a constituent nation - previously, earlier, it was not given to us, but it was by our sacrifices that we earned that - we thought that we could never be divested of the status of a constituent people. But this was violence against law, because Croatia could not unilaterally divest us of that status. We were supposed to be asked. And secondly, it is true that -- the second factor is that the Croatians announced that they would secede from Yugoslavia, and we thought that we had the -- the preemptive right of remaining in the country of our birth, and that that right preempted the right of secession from that country. We had no claims to Croatian towns in which many Serbs lived, but we did have a compact territory which could have been completely separated from Croatia in the way that Croatia was separated from Yugoslavia. There, the population were 80 per cent Serbs. In the area of Knin, Croats accounted for only 7 per cent, whereas now there are no Serbs there at all. In all fairness, not even the Croats are numerous there. Some of them have come there from Croatia and from Bosnia and can go back to Bosnia, if they want.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. With your political struggle for the preservation of the status of a people, what did the Serbs want to achieve? What was their basic objective? And I believe you have partially responded to this question.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Initially we asked -- we demanded cultural autonomy, and there was a referendum for the people to state their views on that. However, the politicians from Zagreb never wanted to talk to us. They started spreading stories to the effect that we were a terrorist party, although nobody had opened fire anywhere, I mean of the members of the Serbian Democratic Party. And they announced that the referendum on autonomy would be prevented by them with all means available. Along those lines, in Benkovac they seized the weapons of the police force in the militia police station, and then they tried to do the same in Obravac, a second Serbian municipality, another Serbian municipality in Dalmatia. However, in Obravac, the people went out in the street en masse and they prevented the weapons from being seized from the police, from the militia. So we opted, thus, for a pen, for a pencil, and they actually wielded, opted for, rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, Mr. Macura, when the first multiparty elections were over, who was the president of the Knin municipality? And what was your post?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Milan Babic was the president of Knin municipality, and I was his deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I did not ask you who was the president of the executive council of Knin municipality.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The president of the executive council was Veljko Popovic. And Minister Markovic, I don't even recall exactly, but we formed normal organs of government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the referendum of Serbs in Croatia. Who was the political initiator of that referendum, and what was its aim? What were its political objectives?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The initiator in chief was Dr. Milan Babic, because he -- it was all launched from Knin, in fact. I am no jurist, but I do know that our legal people were mindful that we should not commit any mistakes in the process. First of all, we embarked on the establishment of a community of municipalities. That was allowed under the valid Croatian constitution. However, we were threatened to the effect that that should not happen, although there was no legal ground for us being prohibited to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here. I'm sorry. You say, according to the constitution, a community of municipalities was allowed to be formed, but "they threatened us." Who threatened you, and how?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They sent the police from Zagreb at us, all the time. They never wanted to politically talk to us. So it was Mr. Bojkovac who was actually and practically in charge of us, and he was the Minister of the Interior in Zagreb. I never went to such talks, but Dr. Babic regularly did and had such talks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to this concrete attitude towards the community of municipalities, what was the attitude of the Croatian political and state top leadership towards the SDS and its political initiatives for cultural autonomy and the like?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, to give you a detail from the work of the Croatian Assembly, when Radoslav Taniga was delivering his address, Glavas threatened him in parliament with a pistol. And later Glavas's claim to fame was that he was a criminal who committed crimes over Serbs in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Radoslav Taniga there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Radoslav Taniga was elected a deputy to the Sabor, to the Croatian parliament before the -- to represent the Serbian Democratic Party. There were five SDS deputies to the Sabor, and there were a number of Serbs from Racan's party who would later also shift to the SDS. Glavas also was a deputy to the Croatian parliament, but of course an HDZ deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear about the signing of any petitions that referred to SDS members?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: This was in Sibenik. Everybody knew about it. Practically the whole town, about 20.000 people, signed a petition for Dr. Raskovic, Branko Popovic and Marko Dobrijevic to be expelled, so that they had to leave Sibenik, even though Dr. Raskovic had spent his entire working career in Sibenik and had a house there in Primosten that is, and he had a flat in Sibenik proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But, Mr. Macura, they never state in the petition that they asked for their expulsion. What they say is: "You have humiliated us -- you have insulted us and deeply humiliated us."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is this really your job to tell the witness the contents of this petition? Sorry for that interruption. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I actually didn't mean to ask the witness to testify about the content of the petition. He characterized the petition as expulsion, and I want to present to him that the actual text of the petition is different so as to elicit his view on it, because the petition says: "You have insulted us and deeply humiliated us. We would be happy if you left this community forever."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Judge is saying to you, Don't tell the witness what is in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You are being told not to say to the witness what is in the document and you go ahead and say so in your answer. Why do you do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not understand His Honour properly, because if.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you don't answer and then say exactly what he says you shouldn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Moloto, I don't see why you should raise your voice at me. I am doing my job. My question might be improper or wrong, but I am doing a very hard job in a very responsible manner. I just explained that His Honour Judge Hoepful nodded his head, and I took that to mean that he understood my motive, why I was proceeding this way. So then I would like to explain to you that this is a case of misunderstanding. Of course I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm telling you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to observe your admonitions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- we are all doing our jobs here and we're all trying to do our jobs properly here, and you're not being very helpful in that direction, because you are being asked by a Judge not to do something and you go ahead and do exactly the same thing. And that is why I am raising my voice. Let me just tell you one thing: It is not for you to tell me when and when I may not raise my voice. Is that okay? Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I won't have anyone raise their voices at me in or out of court. Of course, it is yours to maintain order in the courtroom, but not raise your voice, because I am standing behind this microphone trying to explain what it is that I am doing, and I am just asking you to give me the same treatment as Defence counsel as to all -- everybody else. But, of course, you can take all measures that you deem appropriate within your purview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not for you to tell me whether I may do so. I will do so if I have to. And it is not for you to tell me that nobody will raise his voice for you. I will raise my voice if there is a need. You have raised your voice in this court so many times at me. Now you are going to ask your questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and you are not going to tell the witness what is in that document. The witness has told us what he thinks is in that document, and that's it. And if the witness doesn't say the correct thing that's in the document, it is not for you to correct him. You are leading your witness; you are not cross-examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to this petition. What were its revelations?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: It was not the only case practically, but the whole thing actually boiled down to the Serbs having to leave Croatian towns. And, for instance, we in Knin, in Knin municipality, used to have 20.000 people more before these events, because -- we had 20.000 people flock into Knin because people had to leave Zadar and other smaller towns. This happened also in other cities. People also left Rijeka, so that people flocked into Serbian cities. And this happened throughout the area. Eminent Serbs would have been just taken away and never returned, and every now and then we would hear that this or that person has gone missing, so that this was a massive scale phenomenon. This was no exception. That was the clear message of the Croatian authorities of what their intentions were. They chose renowned Serbs, not just an ordinary man in the street. So, of course, this was normal because this reverberated much more strongly on both sides, showing that their intentions were very serious, to expel Serbs, to kill them. That pavilion, 22 in Zadar, there was a film made also about it. So things are already known. And from this vantage point it is much easier to talk about all these things, because many things have been uncovered since. For instance, Sisak was an horrendous scene, because Serbs were killed in Sisak every step. If you meet any person from Sisak, they will tell you that they know at least 50 people, Serbs, who were killed in Sisak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait a bit, Mr. Macura. Many people were killed in Sisak, but there were no combat operations in Sisak.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: There were no combat operations. I'm talking about Croat towns where there was no combat activity. Just like that, people were rounded up and killed for no reason at all, just because they were not Croats and there were no combat activities in Sisak, just like there were none in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when this referendum was scheduled about the sovereignty and autonomy of the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I think the exact date is the 19th of August. However, two days earlier police forces from Zagreb removed weapons from Benkovac, and they tried the same in Obravac. However, the people prevented it there, the citizenry prevented them. Then barricades were put up, because they had threatened to stop the referendum using all means. So they were going to stop the people from coming out to vote for the sovereignty of Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They said they would prevent it by all means. Who threatened?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Minister Bojkovac was in charge of that. I have said already politicians from Zagreb did not wish to talk to us, although we had won the elections in those areas. But we were practically at the mercy of the Croat police who had labelled us terrorists, although we had not attacked or shot at anyone. When you put up barricades, that is a defensive action. You are not attacking anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will come back to that. You said you were at the mercy of the Croat police, the whole people. What was the name of the Croatian police at the time? Did they change their name?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They changed their uniforms. They changed their name. They called themselves by their new Croat term for the police, which was Redarstvenik. In fact, it was a throwback to the Second World War, the regime of Ante Pavelic. They wanted to show, by every means possible, that they were continuing the ideas and the work of their leader from World War II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on the 17th August, 1990? That's two days before the referendum.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I was in Knin, of course. And after the raid in Benkovac, when we got reports that barricades were being erected in certain villages, we wanted to restore some order, because at that moment chaos reigned and barricades were an obstacle to us. If every village has a barricade around it, then you cannot have any communications.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you specify who sent those reports?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Ilic and somebody from Padjeni let us know that people threw logs over the roads to prevent raids by the Croatian police. And then word of it got out and in other villages they did the same. It spread quickly. And since it was already a state of emergency, we, at the level of municipality, established a Crisis Staff, and the Crisis Staff was headed by the president of the municipality, Milan Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the state of emergency. Who proclaimed it, and when?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Later, Milan Babic practically proclaimed the state of emergency, and I told him it made no sense because he was not entitled to; he didn't have the right to proclaim a state of emergency because he was not head of state. He answered me that it was all the same, state of emergency or the state of war. He created it as the state of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that decision taken by Babic? When did he proclaim it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: On the 17th or the 18th of August. It was on the eve of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that 17th or 18th of August, 1990, you had what position in the municipality of Knin?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I was vice president of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th or 18th of August, how did Milan Babic exactly proclaim the state of emergency? How was it promulgated?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: He called up Radio Knin on the telephone, the Serbian Radio Knin, and told them to announce it. We didn't even know that he was going to do it. But he made that telephone call, so that Serbian Radio Knin announced it. It was on the air. Everybody in Knin heard that the state of emergency had been proclaimed, and people were frightened. But Milan Babic himself left Knin; I didn't even know where he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I am not following correctly, apparently. I had thought that the earlier evidence of the witness was that Mr. Babic had intended to create a state of emergency, but it was pointed out that he didn't have the relevant power to do so and therefore he decided to create a state of war. But now the witness appears to be speaking about a state of emergency. I am a little bit confused. Could I get some clarity, or is it my disability? I would like to know. I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is -- in fact, your suggestion is quite fair. I will try to clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you explained a moment ago in one of your previous answers that Mr. Babic declared a state of war, gave instructions to have it declared by telephone.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Because Mr. Babic didn't know that he did not have the authority, the right, to proclaim a state of war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you tell him that he didn't have the right, after he declared it or before?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: After he declared it, because I hadn't known of his intentions. And he called me on the telephone, but he did not give me a number at which I could reach him. And I told him, "Look, I stayed behind here as your deputy and I'm standing in for you as president now," which means that I practically became chairman of the Crisis Staff, because the president himself was not present in Knin. So it was left to me to deal with the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the factual situation in Knin on the basis of which Dr. Babic proclaimed the state of war? What was the immediate reason for that decision he made? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I believe the immediate reason was the announcement from Zagreb that they would use every means possible to stop the referendum from taking place. There were reports that helicopters had been sent, some freight vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough. You say that Mr. Babic gave instructions on the telephone to have the state of war proclaimed and "I stayed behind in the municipality." Where did Mr. Babic go? Can you explain that? What happened with him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I learned about that later. At that time he was in Trnica, about 15 kilometres from Knin. It's not far from the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give these instructions from Trnica or from Knin?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I cannot know precisely, and that doesn't matter that much now. What matters is that he was no longer in Knin at the time and I was in a position to stand in for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why wasn't he in Knin at that moment?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, he's no longer among the living and we can't ask him, but he must have been afraid and withdrew from the town. But I cannot be certain, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the state of war was proclaimed in Knin municipality on the air, what provisions did you apply, the provisions regulating a state of war or state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: First of all, I told the people that there should be no panic, that we were going to talk, not wage war. And for two nights I was there at the barricades. In fact, I led the work on the barricades from the Centre for Information and Alert. I had telephone connection with people at the barricades

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I stop you here. You said the state of war was proclaimed, a Crisis Staff was established in the municipality, and, due to the absence of Mr. Babic as president of the Assembly, you took over his functions while he was absent.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes, that was stipulated by the rules.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What functions exactly did you discharge in this Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Since, according to the statute of the municipality, Mr. Babic was president of the Crisis Staff, I was his vice president, that is, his deputy, and in his absence I was practically the president of the Crisis Staff myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we continue to discuss the activities of the Crisis Staff, I will ask you one question. You said, "I told the people that there should be no panic, that the situation would calm down." How did you explain that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I appeared on radio and television. After that first night, which was truly a night of sheer panic - all sorts of reports were coming in and people needed to be calmed down - after that night, I expressed my gratitude to the Croat police force for not opening fire at our people, although there was a certain amount of provocation in one place. This Honourable Trial Chamber is probably not familiar with that territory. But on the Krka River, between Raducic and Ivosevci villages, there is a crossing called Brijan. And in that spot Croat policemen fired several rounds at our people who were up there on the hill, because the canyon of the Krka River is very deep. Then, Nedjo Korolija called me on the phone and he was seized by panic. He told me, "They're shooting. What shall we do?" I told them, "Don't you worry. They are deep in the valley. Do not respond to fire if they continue to shoot. If they continue trying to provoke you, don't respond. And only if they advance at you, only then may you return fire." However, the Croat policemen did not continue and the whole incident did not result in a skirmish.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that from this Crisis Staff you maintained communications with people. What means did you use for that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Telephone lines, military lines that can be set up in the field. I do not know the technical side of it, but I had a telephone line with them. I could talk to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said barricades appeared first in one place and then in a whole series of other places. What was the task, the purpose, of the Crisis Staff in relation to those barricades?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: We had to establish some sort of order, and I personally went to Padjeni village. There was a car there with some foreign tourists in it, and the car was unable to leave the area because on one side there were barricades and on the other side there were barricades, and those people didn't know where to go. So I told our people, "Let them pass through. Let them go towards Lika." And that was no problem. The people understood and let them go, and I told them further that it would only hurt us even more if we make trouble for foreign tourists. We already had our hands full with the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you went to Padjeni yourself. I suppose you saw the people manning the barricades. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They were peasants, farmers, people who felled a couple of trees and put up this roadblock. And they didn't have any particular weapons that amounted to much. A couple of hunting rifles, that's all. And I told them that I tried to establish some sort of order. But on day three I was practically replaced from my unofficial post as commander of the barricades. Mr. Babic called me and told me that I could go home, because I had already had a couple of sleepless nights. So I went home. I took my son to have him transferred to Kupres, in Bosnia, where he would stay with his uncle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were your children at the time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: One was nine and another was 14. And since I had a feeling that even worse things were coming, there would be gunfire, I thought that it's better to send my sons to Bosnia, because they had an uncle in Sarajevo and Bosnia was peaceful, quiet at the time. My wife is a pediatrician and I had my own job as a teacher. And I actually volunteered as vice president of the Assembly. I wasn't paid for that post. My actual job was to be a teacher, although at that time I was unable to go to school and teach. But at any rate, we thought we would send the children away to a safer place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that barricade in Padjeni, were you able to learn something about other barricades? Who put them up? Who manned them?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The citizenry themselves, after those unfortunate events in Benkovac and Obravac, in every village you will always find people who are ready to take some action. And then they wanted to earn some credit, I suppose. And at any rate, at the very beginning, the people were organising themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th, 18th and 19th, and while you were president of the Crisis Staff, did the police in Knin have anything to do with it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: At that time, no. Only later did the police take that over. The barricades were removed and checkpoints were set up in several places. The way it was at the beginning, we had those barricades all over the place and we were tripping over them ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In this situation, when the state of war was declared and the roadblocks were set up, the scheduled referendum on the sovereignty and independence of the Serb people, was it held?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes, it was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the result?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: A large majority of the people opted for the autonomy of the Serb people in Croatia. So we did everything at the level of Croatia. Nobody said anything about Serbia or any other republic. What we wanted, what we thought was that we had a right to an autonomy within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, whose political idea was it to set up this community of municipalities and to hold this referendum?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The leading man in this was Milan Babic and he was in charge of everything. But he had his associates that he did this with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This view that he held, was it a view that you yourself supported?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I supported this view fully. I was with Mr. Babic throughout all this, and we actually parted ways only in 1993. But at that time we did not hold the same functions that we did in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, "I was with Mr. Babic throughout this period until 1993 when we parted ways." In what capacity were you with him?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: First, as the vice president of the municipality, I was his deputy in other words; and later on I was in charge of the department of information, I was the Minister of Information, in the SAO Krajina cabinet. Later on, it was to become the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We will go back to the SAO Krajina and the RSK cabinet.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: But I was also in the also in the Krajina Assembly. I don't want to boast, but I won the most votes at the elections for the Assembly of Krajina. And I was, in fact, elected the head of the foreign affairs committee. This is the post that I held in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
