utterances.text: Thank you. When I spoke about your cooperation with Mr. Babic, your work together with him, I wanted to ask you whether your knowledge of languages had anything to do with your -- in your relationship with Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, my knowledge of foreign languages was something very important, that's for sure. But Mr. Babic also knew that I would not be stabbing him in the back regardless of what happened. So he trusted me fully. I accompanied him to all the talks, the negotiations with the international community, United Nations representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, this should be clear already, but let us remove any problems. Were you acting as Mr. Babic's interpreter at those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes. I also performed that function, but there were situations when other people did that. But he always asked me to accompany him, lest somebody should trick him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. December 1990, what would be the event that marked this period? Why do you remember that period?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: On the 19th of December, that was St. Michael's Day, we set up the government of Krajina and that's when we took our oath of office. We were ministers, although we were not paid. We did other jobs, but we also were ministers on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that the government of SAO Krajina was set up. Did Krajina have some kind of a statute, a constitution, law, decision, anything that could form a legal basis for that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: It had its statute, and later on when it became a republic, it had its constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When we talk about the SAO Krajina on the 19th of December, 1990, what was Krajina, in accordance with its statute? How was it defined?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: It was a Serbian autonomous region within the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that after the establishment of the SAO Krajina, that the government was also established and that you held a post in this cabinet. In early 1990/1991, this government, and I particularly mean Mr. Babic, was it active on an international level?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, we were active on the international level. We went to Geneva, to the United Nations there, and we presented our case there. Dr. Babic said that the HDZ was arming -- that the Croatian Democratic Union was arming itself, and that they used the SS troops as their model. And we asked for the protection of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the HDZ was arming itself using the SS troops as their model, that that's what Mr. Babic said. What SS troops was he referring to?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: He was referring to Hitler's SS troops in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any reaction to this information that he provided? You said that you were asking for protection.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: From what I was able to gather, the audience was shocked. Everybody was in a state of shock when he read this out. There was a general consternation in the audience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Was this statement by Mr. Babic accurate? Did you have any knowledge of these facts?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: My feeling was the same -- similar to Mr. Babic's, because a political party cannot establish its own troops. It is not something that would be usual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I was aiming at something else with my question, but it was not precise enough. My question is whether Mr. Babic's claim that the HDZ was establishing its own troops, party troops, was it based on facts, or not?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, of course. The HDZ never tried to even hide this. They had no reason to hide these facts, because they knew that they had support. They knew that they would get the support of Germany and the Vatican for sure, so that they had no problems there. Because Yugoslavia was destroyed from the inside but also from the outside, just as much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, "Of course," they had no reason to hide this. What is it that they had no reason to hide? And how did they not hide it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, the fact that they were arming themselves. They distributed weapons to the members of the parliament, and there are lists. You can see the names of the members of the parliament and the weapons that they were issued with the numbers, serial numbers. And then I don't know how the events developed date by date, but a film was made on how weapons were imported from Hungary, and we in Knin, there were about 500 of us and we were in a hotel, and we watched a videotape that was made by the military security service of the Yugoslav People's Army. They made this film about how weapons were imported from Hungary while Croatia was part of Yugoslavia. It was not internationally recognised at that time. And we listened to what Martin Spegelj was saying, how -- what action needs to be taken, how to knock on the Serbs door, how to shoot them, how to break down the doors. So we simply could not understand how something like that could happen in a state that is still there, that is still functioning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, according to the allegations made in this film, who imported the weapons, and for whom?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, the HDZ, as the party in power, organised the importation of weapons and they armed themselves in order to be able to wage a war, of course the war against Serbs. Because Tudjman himself said, in May 1996, that the Serb issue has been solved in Croatia and that there shouldn't be more than 3 per cent of Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that together with Mr. Babic you went to Geneva to inform them about how those SS troops were established and how the HDZ was arming its troops. Do you know what happened at Plitvice in the first half of 1991? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three hours before the clashes in Plitvice occurred, I crossed through Plitvice. I was driven from Vojnic by -- in a car by a driver named Diego. I know that there was heavy snowfall at the time. At one point he almost skidded off the road. He wanted to hunt rabbits with the headlights, and I said, "Well, there's too much snow there." There were some army troops at Plitvice -- there were some Croatian troops at Plitvice, but they didn't stop us because they didn't want to reveal their presence. It was on Sunday, Easter Sunday. That's when the clash occurred. Why do I insist on the fact that this is a very long process and why history is so important in this area? The first victim of this attack by the Croatian police at Plitvice was Rajko Vukadinovic. His grandfather had been killed, his throat had been slit by the Ustashas in the Second World War. So history repeats itself both at the collective and at the individual level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding this detail that you just explained to us, does the name Vaso Pecer mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Vaso Pecer was a student of mine in high school. He is the first Serb casualty in the Knin area. And his grandfather was killed by the Ustashas in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say --

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: At his funeral, there were, I think, 20.000 people. I think that 20.000 people attended Vaso Pecer's funeral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that Vaso Pecer was the first casualty in the Knin area, and that his grandfather was killed by the Ustashas. Who was Vaso Pecer, and what was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: He was a Serb from the village of Polica. He was killed by Croats from the village of Kijevo - that's the neighbouring village - and they used to be Serbs but now they were no longer Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This event, these events, did they cause any disturbance in the interethnic relations?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, when all this started with the attack on Benkovac and the roadblocks, the Croats went on to establish police stations in areas where there had been no police stations. But these were not normal police stations with limited personnel. They brought in large numbers of personnel in preparation for an attack. This is what happened in Kijevo, in Sabarsko, and in some other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that in these circumstances the SDS acted in a political way. You said -- let me paraphrase what you said. You said that you had the pen and the Croatian side had the rifle. Did the SDS fan the extremism in any way? Did it support extremists?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: We did not fan the extremism, but there was a very real fear, in light of what the other side was doing, the murders of Serbs in Croatian cities and towns, when there was no war, hostilities, in light of the fact that Serbs lost their jobs en masse, that they had to go back to Krajina, those Serbs that were born there. And Dr. Raskovic, as the representative of the party, would never even dream of speaking about weapons and war at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Raskovic try to talk to the high-ranking officials in the Croatian government?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, he did speak to Mr. Tudjman. Let me just say that Dr. Franjo Tudjman had been a patient of his, so they had a long acquaintance. But their talks never yielded any fruit, because Croatia could not secede without the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, legally speaking, they could not do that, because we were a people in the constitution and we had our say. So they had to violate the constitution. And even after that, they knew that we did not want to leave the state that we were born in. And after all, Tudjman said, "What does it mean? Why should it be important that 30.000 people die for Croatia's independence?" He was not ashamed of those thoughts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Dr. Raskovic spoke with Mr. Tudjman. Was any of their meetings ever made public?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They had secret talks, but somebody taped them and then it was published. So there were different reactions among us. Some supported it; others didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Raskovic had secret talks. Someone taped them and publicised them. Who did the recording and the publicising?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that I heard about it. I wasn't that much interested in it. I never wanted to mind other peoples business.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the effect of the publicising, the political effect on the population of the publicising of those talks?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: It was a very disquieting effect, because practically certain conflicts erupted in the ranks of the SDS and within the leadership of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What specifically?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Dr. Babic established the Serbian Democratic Party of the Krajina, practically eliminating thereby Dr. Raskovic. Dr. Raskovic could no longer be president of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just another question along these lines. Do you think that it was Mr. Raskovic who actually made that talk public?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I never thought about it that way. I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You described the situation, and could one say, talking about the situation in which you lived and worked, that the leadership of the SDS and, generally speaking, Serb representatives in Croatia exaggerated the data coming from the Croatian authorities with a view to sewing panic amongst the Serbs and eliciting a reaction that would be to their benefit?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: We never had any such objectives. I specifically certainly did not. We never exaggerated. That is quite clear from this vantage point, because in Croatia there used to live around a million and 200.000 Serbs and now I'm not sure whether there are 250.000 of them there. So that from this vantage point, in hindsight, it is much easier to judge and perceive those events. Croatia was to be cleansed of Serbs. Not even now can Serbs return to Croatia. I have a relative Nikola Bezbradica; he is 80 years old. In his house there are living Croats from Bosnia who can't return to Bosnia. And he cannot even approach his house, let alone occupy it. He has been suing the Croatian state for 11 years now about that house. And you have such cases, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, were the Ustashas, as a concept, as a notion, ever referred to by the Serbian leadership from Krajina in their speeches?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes. There were instances of that. I tried to avoid doing that, but let me tell you what the attitude of many Croats to that is: They're proud of that. Let me give you an example from a football match between Kroacija, Croatia, and the Partizan football team in Belgrade. When Kroacija, which now is Dinamo, went out on the pitch, the audience, the spectators, were shouting, "The Ustashas, Ustasha." Then the president -- the coach of the team, Mr. Canjuga, said, "Oh, these people are rooting for us. Good."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The president of the football club.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were describing the situation in Knin on the 17th of August. Prior to the 17th of August, the referendum, when the barricades were being erected, was the population instrumentalised in order to erect such barricades, do you think? Was this done by someone in an organised fashion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I think that has nothing to do with it, because the Serbs are essentially a democratic people and they like to do things on their own. So that people instinctively felt danger and organised themselves. Later we reduced to this some normal frame works in order to be able to handle the entire situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say they felt this danger instinctively. Was there any real reason for them to feel that way?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I have to repeat that the seizure of arms from the Benkovac police by the Croatian authorities was actually the primer cap which triggered the events that ensued and the erection of barricades as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see on the monitor, please, now 1D0127. That is the number of the Defence exhibit. Your Honours, my colleagues from the Defence team tell me that this document should have been admitted into the electronic system. I don't have any other particular note, except it is number 1D0127. But I do have the typed text, and it is very short. So in order not to lose time, if I could be allowed to show this text on the ELMO, please, and then we could handle the technical glitch after the break, perhaps, if, of course, Your Honours are agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, you may do so, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Defence counsel has not turned his microphone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have in front of you the English translation of the first page of a book. Can you tell us what the English text says?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: This is the title of a book by Dr. Marco Rivelli, "The Archbishop of Genocide," which I translated from the Italian language into English. Sorry, into Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the B/C/S version instead of the English version now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you see in front of you, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: This is my translation of the book by Dr. Marco Aurelio Rivelli, from the Italian into Serbian, and the Italian is [Italian spoken].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this admitted as Defence -- into the file as a Defence exhibit, please. And you may remove it from the ELMO, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want admitted, Mr. Milovancevic? There are two pages there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this page in B/C/S is the introductory page to the book, and behind it is the translation of that page into English. So I should like to ask that both of these pages be admitted for easier reference, for easier understanding. And I apologize for not being precise enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All the pages are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologize for the late objection, but I wonder what the relevance of just admitting these two title pages is. We would object to the admission of this as irrelevant. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I tried to look at the transcript to see what foundation had been laid for that. I didn't see it. Mr. Milovancevic, would you like to answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we, as the Defence team, having specifically marked these two first pages, I should like to show the witness some documents from these books. So by singling out the title page, I wanted to actually point to the fact and prove the fact that the gentleman who is present here is the translator of that book, as the first page shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, then, why don't you do that when you do introduce what is the content of the book? And then you can do everything together, Mr. Milovancevic. And instead of having so many exhibits, we can then have one exhibit, including these introductory pages and the pages that you are going to refer him to. And at least -- and also having laid -- and also having laid the foundation for what you want to tender into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I accept that suggestion and I withdraw my proposal to introduce these two pages separately. We shall do so at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you translated the book, this book, the title of which we just saw a while ago. Being its translator, you are, of course, familiar with its content. Does the content of the book reflect the facts that you are familiar with from your earlier life, from your personal experience and the experiences of other people?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The facts which are reflected in the book I was only familiar with partially, because I had insight into the records and archival files which are reflected in the book only partially. Dr. Rivelli tried to realistically portray what has happened in Knin from the establishment of the independent state of Croatia from 1941 to 1945, mainly depicting Croatia Ustasha crimes against the Serbs. And it also has 105 photographs where you can see -- on which photographs you can see skeletons and massacred people. So that this has been substantiated by authentic documentations, the statements of officials, of some generals, of some politicians, of some Croatian journalists, so that the book is, in fact, eminently good, probative material for what had happened in the independent state of Croatia, the so-called independent state of Croatia, from 1941 to 1945.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Do you know who is Branimir Glavas?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Branimir Glavas is a deputy to the Croatian parliament. He is from Osijek. He is now on trial, but it is actually proceeding very slowly, for crimes committed in 1990 and 1991. They are dragging their feet, actually. There is abundant evidence of his crimes against Serbs in Osijek, but many witnesses have been intimidated and are afraid to take the stand. But he, himself, has stated, namely he never conceived of the fact that he was an Ustasha. He encouraged his people to state that with pride, and so on and so forth. He often appeared on television so that one could see him often, and I know what he looks like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any of his -- a statement made by him on television which refers to the Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I know that he is constantly repeating this: Say that you're Ustashas. You should be proud of that fact. I could not quote verbatim his statement, but I know what its essence is, because he's been repeating it time and again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the break, two short questions. You say he was a deputy to the parliament of Croatia. What party was he representing there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Of course at any rate it was the Croatian Democratic Union, because there also existed the Croatian Party of Rights, with Djapic at its helm, which is a pro-Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. You say that he ordered Serbs to be killed in Osijek. How can that be, a deputy to parliament ordering Serbs to be killed in Osijek?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Because he hails from Osijek. He was working on his terrain, on his turf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that this is a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, we have been repeatedly told, and we've heard a third warning also today, that we should delve into history less. Could you imagine what the reaction of the Jews would be if the world recommended to them to talk less about the Holocaust?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the relevance of that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance emanates from the fact that the Prosecutor's office is completely ignoring, disregarding, the Ustasha crime as a crime of genocide and as a Holocaust, which external features is more horrible than anything that the world has ever seen. We have seen footage from the Korana bridge, and that is but a minor detail of that crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, let me just warn you that people who you say are Ustashas and committed those crimes are not before our Court, so what you are telling us about them has no relevance to this case. You are, accordingly, ruled out of order. That question is overruled. What's more, the Jews are not in this court either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, you said that in his inaugural address, the programme principals of the HDZ, Mr. Tudjman referred to the independent state of Croatia as an expression of the historical aspirations of the Croatian people. Do you know what the position of Mr. Tudjman was towards Serbs and Jews? Do you know of any of his statements to that effect?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes, I do know of a statement of his about that particular subject, namely he stated that he was happy that his wife was not a Serb or a Jew, which speaks a lot about him as a human being and about what he thinks about other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you think that that represented some sort of a message to the Serbian population of Croatia as well as to the Croatian people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, it is all clear, it is as clear as can be. There is no need even to comment on that statement. It is self-explanatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I think that is not self-explanatory. Could you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If someone says that he is happy that his wife is not a Serb or a Jew, that means that under no circumstances could that person live with someone of that ethnicity. My brother is married to a Croat, and that is no problem at all. He is living with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Part of the sentence expresses, in your view, that that means under no circumstances this person could live with someone of that ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That part where he says that he is happy because of the fact, meaning that he would be unhappy otherwise, if the opposite were the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is this the meaning of the word "happy," or is this your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, "happy," in the Serbian language, has a very clear meaning. The English word "happy" could also mean satisfied. Perhaps it is a milder expression. But when you say "happy," "srecan" in the Serbian language, that is the strongest way you can express that particular feeling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You are a language person. You can maybe translate it, this Croatian word into English, in a more appropriate form.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It might be something like hilarious or ecstatic or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to testify in English, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I feel much better with Serbian. It is one reason. Another reason -- another reason is that here is the defendant and I would like him to listen to me in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then speak in Serbian, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If possible. If not -- if you order me to speak English, I will speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You were asked to give the meaning of the word "happy," or whatever that word is in Serbian, and to translate it. Not to say the entire testimony in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please. Other than this statement that Mr. Tudjman made concerning his being ecstatic that his wife is not a Serb or a Jew, were there any other statements made that were indicative of how he viewed Serbs and related to Serbs? Or is that a singular statement made at a certain time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He has made many statements. I could not follow them all. However, he wrote a book, "The Wasteland of Historic Reality," in which there is a multitude of lies. You cannot even read it because it is a wholesale falsification of history and it is really disgusting to read, let alone debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please stop. Don't go into the quality or nature of it. I just wanted to find out if it was a singular occasion or if there were other occasions. I want to thank you, Mr. Witness, not to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Please go ahead, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm sorry. I forgot that you had been waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While we are with Mr. Tudjman, what is it that is most striking of all the things he wrote in that book you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't deal with it much, nor was I very interested. But Franjo Tudjman had spent time both in a camp and in a prison during the communist regime while being at the same time a product of that communist regime. He was one of Tito's generals, but later he turned coat and became a servant of Croat -- Croatians, Croatian diaspora, that is the Croat Ustasha organisation abroad, because he was on their payroll. And I already mentioned that towards the end of the war his job was to transfer Home Guards and Ustashas into the ranks of the partisans so that they would no longer be on the defeated side, they would be among all the winners, after all the crimes they had committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you gave us a lot of background history, and I don't want to take you off the path where you had quite properly been heading before my intervention. So if you could restore yourself to it, we can keep the pace and keep the focus which you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you say about the sentence: "The fear from Ustashas is exaggerated"? How do you read that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: After all that has happened and all that had been announced, there's no reason to even discuss any exaggeration of fear. And the current situation is very clear. Look at how many Serbs live outside of Croatia now and how many stayed in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where does this quotation you are raising come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a quotation, Your Honour. I asked the witness whether it would be fair to say that fear from Ustashas was exaggerated. That is one of the principal arguments of the Prosecution case, as if history did not exist and as if nothing had ever happened. They say that fear was exaggerated. So I am asking the witness, who lived in that territory at that time, whether he shared that impression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're taking that sentence from the case of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take it from the entire conduct of the Prosecution and the Prosecution case. The genocide did happen; the crimes were committed. And were now the fears in 1991 exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know how much I need to address, but it is, of course, not the Prosecution case that there was not genocide in World War II. We consider that essentially irrelevant to this case. And I would object to Defence counsel repeatedly characterizing the Prosecution positions in a way that, I believe, is meant to be disparaging. I don't think that is appropriate to what we're trying to do in court here, and in this particular case, it is simply not accurate. That is not the Prosecution position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I was answering a question from the Bench. I did not defend this argument mentioned by the Prosecutor from the very start. The Prosecutor says it is beyond dispute that there was a genocide, that there had been a genocide; but what I am disputing is the suggestion that fear from genocide is exaggerated, both linguistically and in every other way. I think this is not a viable proposition. We are trying to respond to one of the arguments of the Prosecution, therefore, by asking the witness whether something had been done for that purpose at the relevant time. And I am sorry if the Prosecution is taking this personally, as my personal attitude towards the OTP. I am just discussing the arguments contained -- the allegations in the indictment and the principal arguments of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, in that event, then, if you are addressing the arguments contained in the indictment, I would like you to direct me clearly to where in the indictment or anywhere in the Prosecution case the sentence "The fear from Ustashas is exaggerated" is mentioned, because that's what I wanted to find out, the specific question you were supposed to be answering from the Bench in the first place. You said to me it's from the Prosecution. The Prosecution disputes it. And so that we can keep them quiet, just give us a reference to their case where they state this statement so that I can order Mr. Black out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, whenever the Prosecution cross-examined any of our witnesses, they asked the same question: Did leaders of the SDS in Serbian Krajina exaggerate the fear from Ustashas among the population and thus fanned their reaction to be used later for attaining some political goals? The same thing happened as early as yesterday, when there was cross-examination of our witness Branko Popovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you refer us to a line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My understanding is that there is no line. It's a theme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Judge Nosworthy has something to say. But even before I pass it on to her, I just want to say, while I will allow you to ask the question relating to the fear from Ustashas, I do agree that you have a tendency - and you did so today - of referring to the Prosecution in a disparaging manner, and I would ask you to stop from doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: A conference is needed. A conference with the other members of the Bench is needed, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, if you will, my observation about the question which you posed is that it was a bit too general. And in terms of addressing the mind of the witness, if you could refer to a particular period that you would like the witness to respond to, because I think that is the context within which the Prosecution put it. So for the record, and just to be clear, if you could put it in that way, I think it would be more appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will try to be as precise as I can. If you please, Your Honour, did I understand you correctly that I can proceed with this line of questioning but not ask this particular question? Shall I deal with the general facts? Because there has been considerable delay since my last question and I can no longer make the connection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I didn't make myself clear. The question in issue which resulted in the objection was the question concerning the exaggeration of fear. So what I'm saying is contextualise it in terms of a period, as the Prosecution had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So it can be clearly understood for the purposes of the record. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to also clarify that the Prosecution has not asked about fear of Ustashas. They're talking about 1990 and whether there was an exaggeration of the fear of the Croatian authorities or the Croat people, but not Ustashas. If he want to puts a question about the Prosecution position, he should try to be more accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. Maybe I should leave it to the learned Judge --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: -- to rule on that matter, because Mr. Black has now taken a different point which is a little bit beyond what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But it is part of the question of being exact when you ask questions, Mr. Milovancevic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Obviously, if Mr. Milovancevic wants to know about Ustashas, I am sure he can ask about Ustashas. For purposes of the trial, I think the Prosecution is interested in knowing about the Croat authorities in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quite understand, Your Honour. I'm sorry about this misunderstanding; that is entirely my doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are now talking about the period from 1990 to 1991. In the course of 1990, one of the events that you mentioned was the speech of Mr. Tudjman in the Vatroslav Lisinski hall. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I followed Mr. Tudjman in many situations simply because I had to, and he made many inflammatory speeches. But what is interesting about this is, just after the HDZ came into power, Serbs were massively dismissed from their jobs, while we in Krajina, where Croats were in the minority, did not dismiss them from their jobs. There was one case involving a teacher from Knin where our court reinstated her in her job. Her name was Darinka Krlic. She had been dismissed from her job as a Croat. She sued the school and she was reinstated. But you could not find analogous cases on the other side, because people were dismissed by scores and hundreds, just because they did not sign a statement of support to the ruling party in their work organisation. Why would any employee or a professional have to sign a statement of loyalty to the political leadership? And then later, when more prominent Serbs began to be liquidated in towns, the situation only deteriorated. You will be able to get evidence about those many killings. They are well documented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Those were everyday goings-on in the territory of the Republic of Croatia in early 1990. What was the attitude to the new -- of the newly elected Croatian authorities, led by the HDZ --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I apologize for that interruption. It is even possible that I misheard, but the sentence "Those were everyday goings-on in the territory of the Republic of Croatia in early 1990," if that was part of the question and not the continuation of the answer, then it is either leading or counsel is just testifying without even bothering to put a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend from the Prosecution is perfectly right. I did make an inappropriate comment as part of my question. It is true that it was not part of the question. It does not have a question mark on it, "These were everyday goings-on in the territory of Croatia," and I shouldn't have included it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was: You were talking about the events in 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you desist, Mr. Milovancevic, from making statements to your witnesses before you ask the question? I mean I have been trying to ask you from the beginning of this trial to stop doing just that and you carry on doing it. I don't know why you do it. It doesn't help to keep saying, "I'm sorry, my learned friend was right and I shouldn't have said that." You have said this so many times that it is becoming an irritant now. Just put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you find it difficult, and I think this Bench must stop you every time you ask questions, but that will mean that for every question you raise, the Bench will have to stop you, because you do it with every question you put.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the new Croatian authorities treat the Ustashas in their public statements and appearances?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I already said that Tudjman made that key statement, namely that the independent state of Croatia, which is a reference to Ante Pavelic's regime, was an expression of the Croat aspirations of the Croatian people. This is self-evident and needs no comment. But I agree it is better to talk about Croatian authorities, not Ustashas, because we would be laying all the blame at the door of one little segment of them. But one of the goals of those authorities was to remove the Serb population from those territories, and they practically succeeded because there are very few Serbs left in the territory of Croatia nowadays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what political objective did the Croatian authorities display their attitude to the Ustasha movement in the Second World War? Why did they need to mention them at all? Do you have an explanation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Of course I have an explanation. We don't have to delve deep into the history of things, but we need to understand it and know it. After the Second World War, the communist regime proclaimed brotherhood and unity, brotherhood and unity between henchmen and victims. And the official writers of history books falsified history. However, we Serbs still knew what actually happened, because not all victims were dead. In every massacre there is always a survivor. Thus, in the massacre in the church in Glina, where 1.567 Serbs had their throats slit - and this is documented by a commission - there was only one survivor by the name of Ljuban Jednak. And of course he had to tell his story later because he was deeply traumatized as the survivor of that massacre, and we knew about similar incidents elsewhere. And let me say one more thing. The ethnic cleansing of Serbs continued under the communist regime, and I will tell you how. In a very perfidious way, a law was passed banning the keeping of goats, meaning the law prohibiting an animal from living. I don't think even very perverse minds could think that up. Why? Because Serbs, whose livelihood was the keeping of goats on the mountains of Velebit and Dinara, would have to leave. This is an area of barren rock and crust where you don't have much choice in terms of source of livelihood. Those people, with their families, had to leave after goats were banned. Another way was the building of military training grounds and removal of Serbs from those areas. Let me mention one example. The training ground in Slunj. And to make it completely clear to the Trial Chamber, Slunj is between Karlovac and Korenica, not far from the Plitvice lakes. The Plitvice lakes are a world-renowned sight and tourist sights, and Serb villages were moved from those places massively, while not a single Croat village was touched. So the ethnic cleansing continued after the Ustasha regime; it continued under the communist regime. And what were the Serbs supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, can I just say, when your lawyer or anybody says "stop," please do stop, okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, I tried to stop you. But I wanted to ask you: Do you know for what reason somebody like Branimir Glavas was allowed to stay on the parliament of Croatia? And why others like him mentioned and referred to Ustashas in 1991? Is there a reason?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Of course there was a reason. One was a message to Croats, what to do, and a message to Serbs, what to expect. I think it's self-evident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see on the screen document 1D0128. I think it should be in e-court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes. It's from that book that I translated from the Italian language. And we see the symbols, the iconography, before which Ustashas gave their solemn oath in front of Ante Pavelic, the cross, the knife and the gun. Those are the symbols and the emblems they used in the oath ceremony. And after they committed crimes, Catholic priests received their confessions and absolved them of the crimes. And Stepinac, their archbishop, was decorated with the highest possible order by Ante Pavelic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us: Is this a passage from this book by Mr. Rivelli that you translated? Can we see the text below the picture?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: 25th of June, 1941. The Ustasha newspaper, Croatian Weekly, published this photograph with the following explanation. "Under the sign of the cross, pistol and knife, symbols of the Ustasha oath, the Croatian movement shall fight and win."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at another document. We will be tendering all of these documents together. This is Defence Exhibit 129. If we can look at it, if you can rotate it. Yes. Can we look at the left-hand side, the left-hand half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This photograph, at the bottom here, on the left-hand side, what does it represent, Mr. Macura?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: This is the knife for killing Serbs, or "Serb cutter" for short. Let me remind the Honourable Trial Chamber that Ante Pavelic, as the leader of the independent state of Croatia, held a session of his government where one of the items on the agenda was the knife. So the government discussed this item, the knife, at one of its sessions. It was on the agenda. Because they discussed what kind of a knife should be designed to make it possible for the executioners to kill people as fast as possible and with as little fatigue as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Macura. What does this picture, then, represent? How does one use this implement?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The upper part is made of leather. This is some kind of a glove. And you put your hand in it and you put your thumb through the hole up there, and then you put your fist together, and then only the blade protrudes. And you can see that the blade is curved in order to make it easier to slit the throat of the victim, because it kind of follows the curvature of the neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell us, now, what Marco Aurelio Rivelli said, what is his explanation, the caption?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The special implement designed by the Ustashas, manufactured by Solingen, a German factory, used for the slaughter of Serbs and Jews in mass slaughters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this Serb cutter? What would be a characteristic detail, in just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I know that in 1991, a Serb cutter was found in Banija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you. Do you know anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But how are you perceiving that this evidence will help the Trial Chamber in the decision-making and the issues that are really before them? We have had rather a lot of evidence about your historical data and 1941 and all of the things, the 25th of June, 1941. It's an implement for slitting the throats of Serbs. Do we need to go this far? How will it assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am trying, through this witness, to not to point to certain facts that, for the Serbs who had survived the Second World War in Croatia were quite known, and I am trying to show the Trial Chamber what it meant for the Serb population, when any public figure referred to the Ustashas to the independent state of Croatia and proclaiming it to be the result of the aspirations, historical aspirations of his people, and what kind of a response it could have engendered. These are really quite shocking facts, that even people who are well informed are not familiar with. This is the hidden truth, and I think that my learned colleagues from the Prosecution, when they referred to this topic, they do not really have a proper insight into the real state of the thing. So I think that this will also assist them to assist -- this will assist them to evaluate the testimony of witnesses, to make them realise why certain witnesses are saying certain things. So the main topic is: What were the Serbs afraid of? And the question is whether their fear was indeed logical, normal or exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you have mentioned before the Prosecution and the Prosecution's view of the evidence. It's the Bench that is important in terms of the issues that have to be determined. So you have to bear that in mind and not referring to getting the Prosecution to understand. It is really getting the Bench to understand and to deal with the issues, right. There's also the fact of not going for the overkill, if you will pardon the pun, and I think that you should take it. That insofar as certain areas of historical background are concerned, the Bench understands what the Defence is trying to place before it, and a tremendous amount of evidence has come. And now you have to be more sparing into how you lead evidence in respect of those areas before the Court and not overflood the mind of the Bench with this type of evidence, when it's only a collateral issue, in effect, and it's not really germane to the substantive issue. I don't think I'm speaking out of turn when I say that. You can take it that the Bench comprehends what the Defence is trying to say in respect of the historical data and how -- or, rather, what it is that Serbs may have been acting upon. But it doesn't mean that you are entitled to go into it in perpetuity ad nauseam. Does it? All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree, Your Honour. But if you permit, this is just one question related to the Croatian term for the police officer, the uniforms worn by the police, and their badges. I fully accept what you have just said, Your Honour, but if you allow me, I do believe that it would be germane and it would contribute to your understanding of the situation of the -- even of the acts of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. But Mr. Milovancevic, if it can be summed up effectively by the witness in three sentences or three paragraphs, let's not have 30 pages of evidence in relation to it. That's what I'm trying to say to you. And I want you to investigate every important issue, but still there has to be a way of gauging and evaluating the areas that you can be more extended on and the areas that you have to be more limited on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I hear what you are saying. Mr. Usher, I mixed up the Defence exhibit markings. Could you perhaps just place one photograph on the ELMO now so that we don't waste any time by trying to find it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you translated Mr. Rivelli's book, can you please tell us who is this man on this photograph, whom does he represent?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: This is a Ustasha soldier from the Black Legion, and he is posing with the heads of a Chetnik that had been cut off. And you can see here the insignia, this hat, the cap that is on this dead head could not have remained there, so it must have been posed. We see an Ustasha soldier with the insignia that the -- that Tudjman reintroduced, and his police officers wore this insignia. And this is why most of the Serbs could no longer agree to remain in the police under those insignia, because they knew what the insignia meant and what it harked back to. The message was quite clear, and as a result few Serbs remained in the Croatian police after this reintroduction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can remove the photograph. I would like to tender these photographs into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The photographs are admitted into evidence. May they please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, did you hear about the letter of the Knin police officers to the public media?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, after the decision that the police officers should wear uniforms that for all intents and purposes were identical to the ones worn by those who had been killing Serbs in the Second Word War, this letter was written and it was sent to the federal authorities in Belgrade, in the essence they said that they refused to accept those uniforms with those insignia and they did not want to remain in such a police force. This is what it all boiled down to. I can't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The political sense, the real life sense of this letter, could it be summed up that this insubordination to the Croatian authorities and the attempts to achieve some other political goals?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: No. I wouldn't characterise it in that way. This was merely an attempt, on their part, to defend themselves against some monstrous evil that had been present for such a long time and that was now coming back in this way. This was just an attempt for the people to defend themselves against this evil; it was self-defence, not insubordination. It was a demand made to the authorities to change this and to use different terms, use different uniforms, insignia. But simply nothing could be done. They could not be swayed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the federal authorities of the Yugoslavia or the Croatian authorities assisted in achieving a "peaceful," in quotation marks, or common sense solution to this problem?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, there were some attempts from the federal level, but the people in Croatia would not listen to anything. They had their plan. They wanted to implement it. There was simply no effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, we would like to -- I would like to move on to another topic now. Do you know anything about the referendum that was held in Krajina in 1990 on the remaining in Yugoslavia, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologizes. The second part was not caught.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, can you repeat the second part of your question? The interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So my question to Mr. Macura was whether he knew anything about the referendum that pertained -- the question was the remaining of SAO Krajina in Yugoslavia, and the unification of Krajina with Serbia. When I asked this question, I more or less quoted the actual topic of that referendum. There were different referenda held, but I just wanted to point the witness to this particular one.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: The main initiator of this referendum was Dr. Babic, and of course at this referendum the people voted, almost 100 per cent of them voted in favour of us remaining in the same state with Serbia. I was in the delegation that went to Belgrade where we wanted to be received in the Serbian Assembly, but we were not received by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here, Mr. Macura.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Just one clarification. The question at page 78, line 5, referred to a referendum in 1990, and I wonder, based on the content of what's just been said, if it was 1990 or 1991. If we could please have a clarification of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were elections held in 1990. This was 1991. If I said it was 1990, then I misspoke. Thank you very much to my learned colleague from the Prosecution. The referendum was not held in 1990 but in 1991, the referendum that was held in April, 1991. So my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you replied to my question, Mr. Macura, which referendum did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: My understanding was that you had misspoken. I was thinking about the referendum on the -- on the unification with Serbia, because I had been on this delegation that went to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how the decision was made on how to phrase the question, the referendum question? And who made this decision?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Babic made most of the decisions. He was the top man. He had his associates, people that he worked with and people that he phrased such things with. He made those decisions, and then they would be tabled at the Main Board of the SDS. They were then discussed, and the decision would be made for this proposal to -- for this question to be asked in this way: Are you in favour of the unification with Serbia or not? Because our hand was forced here. We didn't see a way out of the situation. But at any rate, Belgrade did not give us a green light. We were not even received at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us take this one step at a time. We will get to this, Mr. Macura. In your replies, you said at one point that the question at the referendum was on the remaining -- on whether the SAO Krajina should remain in Yugoslavia, unified with Serbia, and at other times you said that it was only unification with Serbia. What was the question?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I don't know the exact phrasing, but what counted was that we wanted to stay in a state that somebody else was trying to destroy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The referendum was held, and what was the result?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I don't know the percentage, but the vast majority of the people opted for joining with Serbia and remaining in the same state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you both slow down, please. The interpreter is struggling to keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of a delegation was it? Who was on this delegation that went to Belgrade? And why?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Ljubica Vujanic was the head of the commission, and I think that she was in charge of the legal formulation of all the documents that related to the referendum, because she was a lawyer. I am not a lawyer. I know some basic stuff about law, but she, as the head of the commission, was supposed to present this to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here, Mr. Macura. So Mrs. Ljubica Vujanic, yourself, and who else was on the delegation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was the president of the Gracac municipality, she was also there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your task? Why did you travel to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: We went to Belgrade in order to be received at the session of the Serbian Assembly, which was in session at the time, and we wanted to present the results of the referendum to the Assembly and our demands to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the request of your delegation to Serbia on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Our request was for the Assembly of Serbia to accept that referendum and to practically receive us into its state, to be together with it in one state. That is the essence. I don't know how to legally expound that, but that is the substance of our request.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you went there as a delegation of the SAO Krajina. Were you, indeed, received in the Assembly of Serbia? What happened there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: No, they did not at all receive us in the Assembly of Serbia. We only conducted informal talks with the vice president, Borisav Petrovic, who has died since. Then also with Pavic Obradovic, and with Mr. Micunovic, who was a deputy to the Serbian Assembly. So we had informal talks and no reception of any kind. We just stayed with them for these informal talks for a couple of hours, and that was it. But not in the Assembly, on some other premises altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just pause, please. Also, do pause after the question, Mr. Macura. Okay. You can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Macura, perhaps we are a bit tired, but we could really pay more attention to the difficulties the interpreters might have because of that. So was the SAO Krajina delegation received at the session of the Assembly of Serbia, or not?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you manage on that occasion to convey to the Serbian Assembly your request? Were you allowed to do so?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: No, we didn't. No we were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet with Mr. Milosevic on that occasion? He was the president of Serbia at that time.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the delegation member from Gracac, the third member of the delegation? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Actually, she cried, she went into tears. They were quite hysterical because she was so disappointed. We didn't know what to do with her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did she break down in tears?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, she broke down in tears because she had hoped that this referendum that we had conducted would yield a positive result. However, once she realised that that would come to naught, she just wept hysterically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Had the delegation been led to believe that your request would have been favourably looked upon? The request for joinder, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were just hopeful. We hoped. We only hoped that that might be the case, that it might be a positive response. Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In connection with this last question by Her Honour Judge Nosworthy, did the Republic of Serbia have any influence on the conducting of that referendum, the results of which you were taking to that republic?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: No, it had no influence whatsoever, and it showed that by not wanting to discuss it at all, in any way with us. We were just hopeful, as I said, that it would be successful in this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in April, 1991?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when the government of the SAO Krajina was established?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: That was on Michael Mass in December 1991 that the cabinet was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the first government?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes. That was the first one. And then there was the government of the SAO Krajina, the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and I don't remember when it was formed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us not overlap, Mr. Macura. You stated in your replies that the SAO Krajina was proclaimed on the 19th of December, Michael Mass, as you put it. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: That was prior to the promulgation of the Croatian constitution in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They announced that the Croatian constitution in Zagreb would be promulgated in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When was the first government of the SAO Krajina established after the SAO Krajina was established?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked this because of my following question. Do you know that in May 1991 a new SAO Krajina government was established?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: That could have been the government of the republic of the Serbian Krajina, which is not the same. That is then a higher level of organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who set up that government?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Dr. Milan Babic did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Dr. Milan Babic set up that government. How could one man have set up a government?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, this is done everywhere. There is someone who forms the government, and this is the practice the world over; that one man forms a government and assembles the team of associates with whom to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Republic of Serbia had any thing to do whatsoever with the forming of the government of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina or the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: According to what Dr. Milan Babic told me, President Milosevic wouldn't hear about the forming of the government of the SAO Krajina. He practically mocked it. He didn't want us at all to form a government. He wanted us to form something at a lower level, to have some secretaries, or what can we call them, but not a prime minister or ministers and such. That is why he actually -- this conflict between him and Milan Babic arose.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that President Milosevic, the President of Serbia, did not want a government to be formed, on the basis -- on what do you base your knowledge of these details?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: On the basis of what Dr. Babic told me, because he had frequent encounters with President Milosevic. And I only met him -- I was with him only for -- on several occasions because they needed interpretation, speaking the same language so that there was no problem of that kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Mr. Babic, when he talked to you about Milosevic's attitude to the government of the SAO Krajina, did he tell you what his own view to that particular issue was?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, yes, he practically showed his views by his deeds. He insisted that we form a government, and that he be the key person in it, the top man. So that his actions spoke -- his deeds spoke quite loudly. He wouldn't heed anybody's advice. He pursued his own policy to the very -- to the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your attitude, what was your opinion towards such conduct on Mr. Babic's part at that time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, I did not really believe much in that, but I then, on the other hand, could not influence Mr. Babic's conduct. And I could have given him my opinion, but it wasn't really relevant that much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the government of SAO Krajina or the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, did you hold any post?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I was the Minister of Information in that government until it was replaced, and it was replaced in connection with the adoption of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are talking about 1991. Do you recall whether and when Croatia and Slovenia proclaimed their autonomy, their independence, their secession from the state?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They proclaimed their secession quite early on, but had not been -- were not recognised by the United Nations. There was some who recognised it, though. I believe the Vatican and Germany recognised their secession. That was a strong support of the secession of the republics to separate, to break away, from the parent state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened in Yugoslavia after the proclamation of Croatia and Slovenia's secession? Do you remember those events?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I cannot recall the dates because I did not think them important and I did not put them down on paper. But I know that events evolved so that Croatia and Slovenia went to the very end in their intention to carry out this secession, and something happened and I wonder how come that not a single Slovenian has been put on trial before the Tribunal at The Hague, because the Slovenians committed the very first crime, a crime against peace, the crime of the top leader of a state which only gave rise to other crimes as a consequence. And there the conduct of the international community was not in keeping with international law; I have to say this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say the Slovenes were the first to commit a crime. What do you mean? When and how did this happen?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: They killed 138 soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army, 138. If you look at events in the world now and see what Israel did for two of their captured soldiers, you can imagine what that state would do if so many of its soldiers had been killed. However, General Kadijevic forbade this to be published, so that the public was not informed. They knew that some soldiers had been killed but they didn't know the number. And the number of soldiers killed in Slovenia was 138.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that? Please let's have some pauses.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I know that particular figure from my talk with Professor Smilja Avramov because her book -- I translated her book "Opus Dei" into English and I communicated with her because of that. And she told me that, among other things, because she had direct dealings with General Veljko Kadijevic, or was with him in a certain period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened in Croatia after the secession was proclaimed? You said those two republics decided to go to the very end, that is how I remember your words. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, they celebrated. There was an atmosphere, a climate of celebrations in Croatia, because Germany had recognised them and they knew Germany to be a powerful state, and then the Vatican followed suit, and they knew they would eventually be recognised by the United Nations. Being recognised by Germany was no small matter, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to these recognitions that you described, were there any conflicts in the area of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: There were conflicts which started at Plitvice, as I mentioned for Easter -- on Easter. And they smouldered, a low intensity conflict smouldered from that time on all the time, also because -- also because the Yugoslav People's Army played the role of a buffer zone, did not allow wider ranging conflicts to erupt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the Yugoslav People's Army would not allow wider ranging or higher intensity conflicts to break out. But did such conflicts break out?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes, they did break out later because the JNA, too, was attacked by the Croatian side and the JNA could no longer only play its initial role, the one that it started with. Practically it found itself amid a conflict, embroiled in a conflict, with the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Croatia proclaimed its secession in mid 1991. There was a conflict with the Croatian -- the forces. Who was attacking whom then and there? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: I have already mentioned that Croatia formed, after the erection of barricades and the blockade of roads, the roadblocks, and railway track blocks, Croatia formed heavy forces and brought them to the newly formed police stations. I referred to the places of Kijevo and Sabarsko where this was the case. There had never been police stations in those places, but they pulled into them very heavy police forces and they attacked from there the territory of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you have not responded to my question. Perhaps I didn't put it quite precisely. How did the conflict between the JNA and the Croatian forces break out? Who attacked whom there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Well, one could also follow that on television, and other media, because the barracks in Croatian towns were put under blockade. And the soldiers were threatened. Even the wives and children of the officers were brought in front of the blockades, and they threatened that the wives and children of the officers would be killed if the army did not leave the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any armed attacks on the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
utterances.text: Yes, there were attacks. I remember, for instance, the Korana bridge and then the one in Karlovac. There was a horrendous crime --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That will suffice. Thank you. When was this attempt to pacify the situation, with the assistance of the United Nations, through the offices of the -- what is referred to as the Vance plan? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MACURA
